chapter_theme: Theft begins as a thought, and its wish alone is an offence. The chapter sets களவு against அளவு, stealth against measure, as two settled dispositions that can't live together, and promises ruin to the one and heaven to the other.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar reads the chapter as addressed to renunciants: what theft is and that it must be avoided (281-282), the reasons (283-284), its incompatibility with renunciation (285-287), its contrast with virtue (288), how thieves come to ruin (289), and the fruits of both paths (290).

281.reading: One who is called a person wanting not to be scorned should guard his own heart against stealing anything at all.
281.nuance: The verse guards the heart, not the hand, and so the offence is relocated. Parimelazhagar uses எள்ளாமை for a long attack on Lokayata materialism, and this polemic is entirely his.

positions.position: It means not scorning release: the person wants liberation and is respected by ascetics for that.
positions.quote: வீட்டினை இகழாது விரும்புவான் இவன் என்று தவத்தோரான் நன்கு மதிக்கப்படுவான்;

positions.position: It means not being scorned by other people, a matter of ordinary repute.
positions.quote: பிறரா லிகழப்படாமையை வேண்டுவா னிவனென்று சொல் லப்படுமவன்,

282.reading: Even thinking it in the mind is wrong, saying 'we will steal another's goods by stealth'.
282.nuance: Parimelazhagar limits this high standard to renunciants, whose minds he says are special, but the verse names no such group. The distinction matters, as a universal thought-crime is a stronger claim.

283.reading: Gain got by stealth will perish beyond all measure, even as it seems to grow.
283.nuance: ஆவது போல, 'as if growing', places the ruin inside the appearance of success. Parimelazhagar gives அளவிறந்து a sharp sense: as it goes, stolen wealth leaves sin and blame behind and takes earlier virtue along with it.

284.reading: Love that has ripened in stealth yields, at harvest, a sorrow that doesn't die.
284.nuance: The verb and noun suggest a crop: கன்றிய, then விளைவு. Using காதல் for the urge to steal treats theft as an attachment, and Parimelazhagar makes the point that the craving breeds repetition, which is why the sorrow doesn't end.

285.reading: Having a loving nature with அருள் in view isn't found in those who, with goods in view, watch for others' lapses.
285.nuance: The rhyme of அருள்கருதி and பொருள்கருதி sets two objects of attention side by side as if a mind could hold only one. பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார் is a precise picture of the thief's patient watching.

286.reading: Those whose love has ripened in stealth can't keep to the path of அளவு.
286.nuance: The rhyme அளவு and களவு runs through the next several verses, so the chapter has built its argument into one letter's difference.

positions.position: அளவு is reasoned inquiry measuring the soul, karma and release, which he identifies with a Jain term.
positions.quote: உயிர் முதலியவற்றை அளத்தலாகிய நெற்றியின்கண் நின்று அதற்கு ஏற்ப ஒழுகமாட்டார்;
களவின்கண்ணே மிக்க ஆசையையுடையவர் நேரின் கணின்று ஒழுகுதலைச் செய்யமாட்டார்,

positions.position: அளவு is living within limits, and failing to do so leads to theft, which reverses the causal direction.

287.reading: The dark knowledge called stealth isn't found in those who have set their love on the strength called அளவு.
287.nuance: Stealth is granted to be a kind of intelligence, just a dark one, so cleverness alone is not a virtue in the Kural. Parimelazhagar says stealth and renunciation are opposed as dark and light.

288.reading: Deceit stands in the heart of those who know stealth, just as virtue stands in the heart of those who know அளவு.
288.nuance: The comparison gives vice the same stability as virtue. Manakkudavar draws the discouraging conclusion that once learned, stealth can't be given up.

289.reading: Those who know nothing but stealth perish right there, having done what is beyond measure.

positions.position: The ruin is immediate and inward: they are lost the moment they think such thoughts, and 'other things' are the renunciant's permitted food and lay gifts.
positions.quote: அவ்வளவல்லாத தீய நினைவுகளை நினைத்த பொழுதே கெடுவர்;

positions.position: The ruin is civil: kings execute thieves.

290.reading: For those who steal, உயிர்நிலை falls away; for those who don't, the world of the gods doesn't fall away.
290.nuance: The shared verb தள்ளு balances the near against the far, in Parimelazhagar's phrase: even what is closest fails the one, and even what is remote doesn't fail the other.

positions.position: உயிர்நிலை is the body, lost when the king punishes.
positions.quote: களவினைப் பயில்வார்க்குத் தம்மின் வேறல்லாத உடம்பும் தவறும்;

positions.position: உயிர்நிலை is release, so thieves miss liberation just as non-thieves gain heaven.
positions.quote: பிறர் பொருளைக் கள்வார்க்கு உயிர்நிலையாகிய வீடு பெறுதல் தப்பும்;

positions.position: It is life itself, and the gods' world becomes a world of fame.

links.note: Both move the offence to the planning mind: 204 says that merely plotting ruin sets virtue plotting in return, and 282 says that merely thinking of theft is wrong. Parimelazhagar reads the standard in 282 as one for renunciants, while 204 has no such limit.

Both describe prosperity that seems to exist and then vanishes: stolen gain 'as if growing' in 283, and in 479 the life of one who doesn't live by measure, which seems to exist and is gone. Both also turn on அளவு, so here the moral and the economic meanings of 'measure' meet.
659 says that what is taken with tears goes with tears. Together they make the same bet about ill-gotten gain, but 283 stresses its illusion of growth and 659 stresses its justice.

source_issues: 290: the verse text repeats கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, where the sense and all three commentators require கள்ளார்க்குத். As printed, it would promise heaven to thieves. It also has உளகு for உலகு.
288: the verse text has அளவறாந்தார் for அளவறிந்தார்.
287: the verse text has கண்ட இல் for கண் இல் (Parimelazhagar: புரிந்தார்கண் இல்).
283: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse. Kalaignar's entry ends with a stray verse number, 284.
